electrical_engineering.caption: The curriculum is a map: mathematics, physics and programming (blue) feed the core of circuits → electronics → digital → architecture (gold), which branch into the specialisations (pink): signals, control, communication, power, fields and devices. Labs tie it all to the bench.

ee_math.caption: The maths of EE: calculus and vector calculus (fields, Maxwell), differential equations and Laplace (circuit transients), linear algebra (networks, states), complex numbers (phasors, poles), probability (noise) and numerical methods (simulation).

ee_physics.caption: Physics gives EE its meaning: charge and fields (Coulomb, Gauss, Faraday), waves and light, and the quantum and chemistry ideas behind semiconductors and batteries.

ee_programming.caption: Engineers write code for three jobs: firmware that runs on chips (C, embedded C), descriptions of hardware (HDLs), and simulation and analysis tools (Python, SPICE, field solvers).

ee_circuits.caption: Circuits I and II in one map: the basic laws, systematic solution methods and equivalents (left), then time-domain transients, AC steady state, power and frequency response (right).

ee_electronics.caption: Devices first (diodes, BJTs, MOSFETs, CMOS), then what you build from them: amplifiers, op-amp circuits, feedback systems and the converters that bridge analogue and digital.

ee_digital.caption: Combinational logic (left) computes from the current inputs; sequential logic (right) adds memory and a clock. Together they build every processor and memory.

ee_architecture.caption: Architecture connects logic to software: how a CPU executes instructions fast (left), and how a microcontroller talks to the world through peripherals, buses and an operating system (right).

ee_signals.caption: A signal is information in time; a system transforms it. Convolution describes any LTI system in time, and the Fourier, Laplace and z transforms describe it in frequency.

ee_dsp.caption: DSP does signal processing with numbers: transforms and digital filters (left), and the practical issues of sample rates, finite precision and real applications (right).

ee_em.caption: Fields first (statics, Maxwell, waves), then their engineering uses: guiding signals along lines and structures, matching them, radiating with antennas and keeping unwanted interference out.

ee_devices.caption: From atoms in a crystal, to carriers, junctions and transistors (left), to modern devices, light-emitting and detecting parts, and how chips are manufactured (right).

ee_control.caption: Control uses feedback to make a system do what you want: model it, measure how it responds and whether it is stable, then design a compensator (root locus, frequency response, PID, state feedback).

ee_comm.caption: A link: encode, modulate onto a carrier, cross a noisy channel, demodulate and decode. The theory (left) says what is possible; the systems (right) are how it is done.

ee_power.caption: Energy from generator to wall: machines and transformers (left), then the grid, its protection and the power electronics that convert and control energy (right).

ee_labs.caption: Measure (instruments), build (breadboard, solder, PCB) and report (error analysis, safety): the practical skills that turn theory into working hardware.

ee_electives.caption: Specialisations that build on the core: radio and chips, light and wireless on the left; robots, AI accelerators, medical devices and energy systems on the right.

limits_continuity.caption: Slide x toward 0 from the right: f(x) never reaches 0/0 there, yet it closes in on L = 1. That is what a limit means.

integration_techniques.caption: Integration by parts turns ∫x e⁻ˣ dx into −(x+1)e⁻ˣ. Drag b and watch the shaded area match the closed form.

sequences_series.caption: Partial sums of 1 + r + r² + … settle toward 1/(1−r) when |r| < 1. Push r toward 1 and the series barely converges.

vectors_3d.caption: The dot product measures how much two vectors point the same way; the cross product (its z-part, here) measures the area they span. Drag b around a.

partial_derivatives.caption: Fix y at y₀ and you have an ordinary curve in x; its slope is the partial derivative ∂f/∂x. Change y₀ to tilt the slice.

multiple_integrals.caption: A double integral adds up density over an area. The total of a Gaussian blob is ρ₀·π·σ²: widen it or raise its peak and the total follows.

vector_fields_line_integrals.caption: Work along a path is ∮F·dl. For this swirling field, a circle of radius R collects 2πR²: the longer the path with the field, the more work.

divergence_curl.caption: Divergence says how much a field spreads out (outward arrows); curl says how much it swirls. Mix the two sliders: F = (a x − c y, a y + c x).

greens_theorem.caption: Green: the circulation around the square equals the curl summed over its inside. For F = (−y, (1+p)x) the curl is 2+p everywhere, so both sides are (2+p)·4h².

stokes_theorem.caption: Stokes: the circulation around the gold edge equals the flux of the curl through any surface it bounds, flat or domed. Change the dome height; the answer does not move.

divergence_theorem.caption: Divergence theorem: the net outflow through the closed loop equals the total source inside. Here ∇·F = 2k everywhere, so flux = 2kπR².

ode_first_order.caption: y′ + y/τ = u/τ: the quantity creeps from its start toward u, covering 63% of the gap every time constant τ.

ode_second_order.caption: s² + 2ζω₀s + ω₀² = 0. Small damping ζ rings and overshoots; ζ = 1 is the fastest without overshoot; large ζ is sluggish. Here ω₀ = 4 rad/s.

ode_systems.caption: ẋ = A x with A = [[−a, −w],[w, −a]]: trajectories spiral. With a > 0 they spiral in (stable); a < 0 they spiral out (unstable).

laplace_math.caption: The Laplace transform of this decaying cosine has poles at s = −a ± jω. Decay a is the real part of the pole; the ringing frequency ω is the imaginary part.

pde_intro.caption: Heat equation ∂u/∂t = k ∂²u/∂x²: the sharp 3rd harmonic dies 9× faster than the smooth one, so the profile smooths out. Raise k for faster diffusion.

matrices_systems.caption: Each equation of A x = b is a line; the solution is where they cross. When the lines become parallel (p = −1) det A = 0 and there is no unique answer.

determinants.caption: The determinant is the factor by which the matrix scales area (the gold square). It hits 0 when the plane is flattened onto a line: the matrix is not invertible.

vector_spaces.caption: The same vector v has different coordinates in different bases. Change the angle between the basis vectors and watch the coordinates (c₁, c₂) change while v stays put.

matrix_decompositions.caption: SVD says any matrix is rotate–stretch–rotate. Here A = R(φ)·diag(σ₁, σ₂): the unit square becomes a parallelogram stretched by σ₁ and σ₂. A big σ₁/σ₂ means ill-conditioned.

expectation_variance.caption: A binomial count has mean np and variance np(1−p). Change n and p: the centre of the bars follows the mean and the width follows the variance.

random_processes.caption: One realisation of a random process: a 3 Hz tone buried in noise (a fresh noise draw appears every moment). The spectrum below shows the tone standing above the noise floor.

noise_modeling.caption: Thermal noise v_n = √(4kTRΔf): it grows with the square root of resistance, temperature and bandwidth. Compare a 1 kΩ and a 1 MΩ resistor on the log axes.

estimation_theory.caption: Averaging N noisy readings narrows the spread of the estimate by √N. No unbiased estimator can beat the Cramér–Rao bound Var ≥ σ²/N, and the plain average reaches it.

complex_numbers.caption: A complex number is a point (or arrow) in the plane: a + jb in rectangular form, r∠θ in polar form. Drag a and b and watch r and θ update.

euler_formula.caption: e^(jθ) is a point on the unit circle: its real part is cosθ and its imaginary part is sinθ. Turn θ to 90° and you get j; to 180° and e^(jπ) = −1.

poles_zeros.caption: H(s) = K Π(s − zᵢ)/Π(s − pⱼ). Poles (×) are where the response blows up; the closer to the jω axis, the longer the ringing. Poles in the right half-plane are unstable.

contour_integration.caption: The contour integral ∮f dz = 2πj Σ(residues inside). Grow the circle and each pole it swallows adds its residue (each is 1 here) to the answer.

logic_boolean_math.caption: De Morgan's law: ¬(A·B) = ¬A + ¬B. Toggle the inputs: the two sides always agree, so this circuit (their XNOR) outputs 1 in every row.

combinatorics_ee.caption: The bar height at k is C(n,k)/2ⁿ: the number of ways to choose k items from n. These counts are the rows of Pascal’s triangle and the shape of a binomial.

root_finding.caption: Newton’s method rides the tangent line down to the x-axis to get a better guess: x₍n+1₎ = xₙ − f/f′. Start anywhere positive and it homes in on √2 in a few steps.

numerical_integration.caption: The trapezoid rule replaces the curve with straight pieces and adds up the strips. More strips (bigger N) shrink the error; here the exact area is 2.

ode_solvers.caption: Euler’s method steps y′ = −y forward: yₙ₊₁ = yₙ + h f. Small h tracks the exact curve; h > 1 overshoots into oscillation, and h > 2 blows up.

error_analysis.caption: Errors propagate through a formula: for P = V²/R the voltage error counts twice (power 2) and the resistor error once. The worst case adds them; independent errors combine as a root-sum-square.

fourier_math.caption: Any periodic signal is a sum of sinusoids. These are the first N harmonics of a sawtooth (aₖ = 2/πk); more terms sharpen the ramp, and the overshoot at the jump never disappears (Gibbs).

mechanics_kinematics.caption: Newton’s F = ma with only gravity acting: horizontal speed stays constant while vertical speed changes by 9.81 m/s every second. Change launch speed and angle.

energy_momentum.caption: A mass on a spring swaps energy between potential and kinetic while the total stays fixed (k = 100 N/m). The dots show the swap live; power is the rate this energy moves, P = dE/dt.

gauss_law_ee.caption: For a uniformly charged ball, Gauss’s law gives E growing linearly inside and falling as 1/r² outside, as if all the charge sat at the centre. The total flux is always Q/ε₀.

capacitance_physics.caption: C = εA/d: bigger plates, a smaller gap or a dielectric (εr) all store more charge per volt. The energy at 10 V is ½CV².

current_resistance_physics.caption: R = ρL/A: a longer, thinner or more resistive wire resists current more. Copper is 17 nΩ·m; nichrome heater wire is about 1100 nΩ·m.

shapes.text: B into page (×),  electron circles at r = mv/qB

magnetic_fields_forces.caption: The magnetic force F = qv×B is always sideways to the motion, so it only turns the electron: circular orbit of radius r = mv/(eB). More B or less speed tightens the circle.

readouts.label: peak emf N B A ω (A = 0.01 m²)

faraday_lenz.caption: A coil spinning in a field has flux that varies as cos; the induced voltage is its negative slope, so it is a sine 90° ahead. Faster spin, stronger B or more turns give more emf.

inductance_physics.caption: A solenoid’s inductance is L = μ₀μr N²A/ℓ: more turns (squared!) or an iron core (μr large) multiply the energy ½LI² stored in its magnetic field. Here A = 3.14 cm², ℓ = 10 cm.

optics_basics.caption: Snell’s law n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂: light bends toward the normal when entering a denser medium. Going from dense to less dense at a steep angle there is no refracted ray at all: total internal reflection.

photoelectric_effect.caption: Light arrives as photons of energy E = hf. Below the threshold frequency no electrons escape at all, however bright; above it each photon frees one electron with kinetic energy hf − φ.

atomic_structure_ee.caption: Electrons fill shells from the inside out. Chemistry and conduction are set by the outer (valence) electrons: step Z from 10 (neon) to 11 (sodium) to 14 (silicon, 4 valence).

bonding_materials.caption: Resistivity spans over 25 orders of magnitude, set by how freely electrons can move: metals share a sea of electrons, semiconductors have a small gap, insulators a huge one. Bars show powers of ten above copper (NiCr = nichrome, n-Si = doped silicon) (1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m).

batteries_electrochem.caption: The Nernst equation E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q: cell voltage sags as reaction products build up (Q rises) and is E° when Q = 1. Hotter cells and fewer transferred electrons change the slope.

intro_programming.caption: Every program is variables, decisions and loops. Follow the token: it loops while i < n, adding each array element, then leaves the loop and prints the total.

c_language.caption: C source goes through a fixed pipeline: preprocess (#include, #define), compile to assembly, assemble to object code, then link with libraries into one executable you load onto the chip.

data_structures.caption: A binary search tree keeps smaller keys left and larger keys right, so a search for 6 only touches 3 of the 7 nodes (8 → 3 → 6): O(log n) instead of O(n).

algorithms_complexity.caption: Work grows with problem size n. Merge sort, T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), lands at n log n; a naive n² method is fine at n = 10 but hopeless at n = 10⁶.

matlab_python_sim.caption: A typical simulation script: build a signal, add noise, take the FFT. The spectrum below is exactly what numpy.fft.fft would show: peaks at 5 Hz and your chosen second tone.

embedded_c.caption: A hardware register is just a row of bits. Click a bit to flip it: setting bit n is REG |= (1<<n); clearing it is REG &= ~(1<<n). Each bit might be one pin or one feature.

hdl_verilog_vhdl.caption: assign y = s ? b : a; is a 2-to-1 multiplexer: s picks which input reaches y. An HDL line like this describes real gates, not steps executed in order.

simulation_tools.caption: SPICE turns a circuit into equations: it builds a conductance matrix from the netlist and device models, solves it at each time step (iterating for non-linear parts such as diodes) and plots the node voltages.

field_solvers.caption: A field solver finds the potential V that satisfies ∇²V = 0 inside the box with the top edge held at V volts and the other three grounded. Add series terms (or mesh cells) for a closer answer.

electrical_basics.caption: Power is voltage times current: P = V·I, and energy is power times time. Raise either V or I and the dissipated power climbs; a 12 V, 2 A load draws 24 W.

kcl.caption: KCL: charge cannot pile up at a node, so what flows in must flow out. Set three currents and the fourth is forced: I₄ = I₁ + I₂ − I₃ (negative means it really flows the other way).

kvl.caption: KVL: going once around a loop, the voltage rises (battery) equal the drops (resistors). Change any resistor: the 12 V is shared out in proportion to resistance.

series_parallel.caption: Series resistors add: R_s = R₁ + R₂. Parallel resistors give more paths, so the total is always smaller than the smallest one: R_p = R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂).

voltage_divider.caption: Two resistors share the input voltage in proportion to their sizes. Slide R₂: Vout climbs from 0 toward Vin. At R₂ = R₁ it is exactly half.

current_divider.caption: Current prefers the easier path: the smaller resistor carries more. The two branch currents always add back to the total, I₁ + I₂ = I.

nodal_analysis.caption: Nodal analysis: write KCL at each node and solve G·v = i. Here the conductance matrix is [[1/R₁+1/R₂, −1/R₂], [−1/R₂, 1/R₂+1/R₃]]. Resistors are in kΩ, currents in mA, so voltages come out in V.

mesh_analysis.caption: Mesh analysis: write KVL around each loop with a loop current, then solve R·i = v. The shared resistor R₂ carries the difference i₁ − i₂. Resistors in kΩ give currents in mA.

shapes.text: output voltage at the joined node (V)

superposition.caption: Superposition: in a linear circuit, the output with both sources on is just the sum of the outputs with each source alone (the other turned off). The two coloured parts stack to the total.

thevenin_norton.caption: Any linear source looks like a voltage Vth behind a resistor Rth (or a current IN = Vth/Rth across it). The operating point is where the source line meets the load line.

max_power_transfer.caption: Load power is highest when RL = Rth (the load matches the source), and then half of all the power is lost inside the source: efficiency is only 50%.

source_transformation.caption: A voltage source Vs in series with Rs and a current source Is = Vs/Rs in parallel with Rs make the exact same terminal line, so either can replace the other when analysing the rest of the circuit.

dependent_sources.caption: A dependent source is controlled by another voltage or current: here the current source delivers i = gm·v. Dropping it across a load RL makes a voltage amplifier with gain −gm·RL.

capacitor_ee.caption: i = C dv/dt: the current is largest when the voltage is changing fastest, so the capacitor current leads the voltage by 90°. Higher frequency or bigger C lets more current through (smaller reactance).

inductor_ee.caption: v = L di/dt: the voltage is largest when the current is changing fastest, so the inductor voltage leads the current by 90°. Higher frequency or bigger L raises the reactance.

rc_transient.caption: v(t) = Vf + (V₀ − Vf)e^(−t/RC). In one time constant τ = RC the capacitor covers 63% of the way; after 5τ it is essentially done. Bigger R or C slows it.

rl_transient_node.caption: An inductor refuses sudden current changes: i(t) = (V/R)(1 − e^(−tR/L)). The time constant is τ = L/R; more inductance slows the rise, more resistance speeds it up. (V = 10 V.)

rlc_transient.caption: A series RLC (L = 10 mH) responds to a 1 V step: s = −α ± √(α²−ω₀²). Low R rings (underdamped) with decay α = R/2L; raise R and the ringing dies, then turns sluggish.

damping_regimes.caption: Same circuit, three flavours: under-damped rings, critically damped reaches the final value fastest without overshoot, over-damped crawls. Drag ζ to move the gold curve between them.

sinusoids_ac.caption: A steady AC signal is set by three numbers: amplitude Vm, frequency f and phase φ. Positive φ shifts the wave to the left (it leads). 170 V peak at 60 Hz is the 120 V rms mains.

impedance_admittance.caption: Impedance Z = R + j(ωL − 1/ωC) generalises resistance to AC. Below resonance the capacitor dominates, above it the inductor does; at resonance the reactances cancel and |Z| dips to R.

rms_average_power.caption: The power pulses at twice the line frequency; its average is Vm²/2R, the same as DC at Vrms = Vm/√2. That is why an AC outlet of 230 V rms heats like 230 V DC.

complex_power.caption: Complex power S = P + jQ is a right triangle: P (real) does the work, Q (reactive) sloshes between source and load, and S = VI is what the wires must carry. The angle φ is the load’s phase.

power_factor_node.caption: Adding a capacitor bank cancels reactive power Q without changing the real power P, so the apparent power S (and the current in the supply wires) shrinks. Pink = before, green = after.

three_phase.caption: Three sinusoids 120° apart sum to zero, which is why a balanced three-phase system needs no return current. Shrink phase C to unbalance it and a neutral current |1 − m| appears.

transfer_function_ee.caption: H(s) = Vout/Vin tells you how every frequency is scaled and delayed. This second-order response has complex poles: low ζ gives a resonant peak near ωn; high ζ rolls off smoothly.

frequency_response_bode.caption: A Bode plot shows gain (dB) and phase against log frequency. Each pole bends the gain down by 20 dB per decade and adds up to 90° of lag. Move the poles and the gain.

resonance_q.caption: A series RLC passes the most current at f₀ = 1/(2π√LC). The quality factor Q = ω₀L/R measures how sharp the peak is: low resistance gives a tall, narrow resonance.

high_pass_filter.caption: A high-pass filter H = sRC/(1+sRC) blocks DC and passes fast signals: below the corner 1/RC the gain climbs at +20 dB/decade, above it the gain is flat at 0 dB.

band_pass_filter.caption: A band-pass filter passes a window around ω₀ and rejects both lower and higher frequencies. Raising Q narrows the window (bandwidth = ω₀/Q).

notch_filter.caption: A notch filter nulls one frequency, such as 50/60 Hz hum, and leaves everything else alone. A high Q makes the notch narrow so little useful signal is lost.

two_port_networks.caption: A two-port hides everything inside and keeps only the relations between port voltages and currents. For this T-network the open-circuit impedance parameters follow directly from the resistors.

mutual_inductance.caption: Current changing in coil 1 makes flux that threads coil 2 and induces v₂ = M di₁/dt. The coupling k (0 to 1) is how much of the flux links; the gold flux lines fade as k drops.

transformer_ideal.caption: An ideal transformer scales voltage by the turns ratio n = N₂/N₁ and current by 1/n, so power in equals power out. Step-up (n > 1) raises voltage and lowers current.

laplace_circuit_analysis.caption: In the s-domain a series RLC (L = 10 mH) becomes algebra with Z_L = sL and Z_C = 1/sC. Its poles are the roots of s² + (R/L)s + 1/LC (units: krad/s): they pair up on the real axis when R is large and split into a complex pair when it is small.

readouts.label: intrinsic carriers vs Si at 300 K

energy_bands_ee.caption: A solid’s band gap Eg decides its character: near 0 it is a metal, ~1 eV a semiconductor (silicon is 1.12 eV), several eV an insulator. Heat lifts electrons across the gap, ∝ e^(−Eg/2kT).

doping_pn_material.caption: Doping floods the crystal with one carrier type (n ≈ N_d), which suppresses the other through n·p = nᵢ². Heat raises nᵢ, so minority carriers grow with temperature.

drift_diffusion_ee.caption: Carriers move two ways: drift down an electric field E (J = qμnE) and diffusion down a concentration gradient (J = qD dn/dx). Here n falls off with length L from n₀ = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ (electrons in Si, μ = 1350 cm²/Vs).

pn_junction_ee.caption: Forward bias (right) lowers the barrier and current explodes exponentially; reverse bias (left) leaves only the tiny saturation current. Doubling Is or n shifts the knee.

diode_models.caption: Three models of the same diode: ideal (a one-way switch), constant-drop (a switch plus ~0.7 V) and exponential (the real curve). The small-signal resistance r_d = nV_T/I_D shrinks as current rises.

rectifiers.caption: A diode passes only one polarity. A half-wave rectifier keeps half the cycle; a bridge flips the negative half, doubling the ripple frequency. Each diode steals about 0.7 V.

clippers_clampers.caption: A clipper slices off everything above (or below) a chosen level; a clamper adds a DC shift so the whole waveform sits above, say, 0 V. Both are just diodes plus a reference or a capacitor.

zener_regulation.caption: Above its breakdown voltage the zener clamps the output at Vz. Below the point where the divider reaches Vz it does nothing. Load and series resistance set where regulation starts.

led_photodiode.caption: An LED’s colour is its band gap: λ(nm) = 1240/Eg(eV). A 1.9 eV gap gives red (650 nm); 2.7 eV blue; infrared needs under 1.7 eV. A photodiode runs this in reverse: absorbed photons make current.

bjt_regions.caption: A BJT’s collector current is β times the base current once VCE exceeds ~0.2 V (active region); below that it saturates. The slight upward tilt is the Early effect. Cutoff is IB = 0.

bjt_biasing.caption: A voltage-divider bias fixes V_B ≈ 12·R₂/(R₁+R₂) (R₁ = 47 kΩ), so I_E ≈ (V_B − 0.7)/R_E barely depends on β. The operating (Q) point sits where that current meets the load line.

bjt_small_signal.caption: Around a bias current the BJT behaves like a controlled source: gm = I_C/V_T (about 39 mS per mA), r_π = β/gm, and a collector resistor turns it into gain A_v = −gm(r_o ∥ R_C).

bjt_amplifiers.caption: Same transistor, three connections. Common emitter (1) gives large gain and flips the sign; common collector/emitter follower (2) has gain just under 1 and a low output impedance; common base (3) gives gain without inversion.

bjt_switch_node.caption: As a switch the BJT is either cut off (V_in < 0.7 V, output = 5 V) or driven hard into saturation (output ≈ 0.2 V). Enough base current (small R_B) guarantees saturation.

mosfet_physics_ee.caption: A positive gate voltage pulls electrons to the surface under the oxide. Once V_GS passes the threshold V_T an n-type channel connects source to drain, and a thicker channel (bigger overdrive) conducts more.

mosfet_iv.caption: Below V_DS = V_GS − V_T the MOSFET acts like a voltage-controlled resistor (triode); above it the current saturates at ½k(V_GS−V_T)² and the curves go flat. Raise V_T or lower k to shrink them.

mosfet_biasing.caption: Source degeneration stabilises the bias: the device curve and the resistor line cross at the operating point. If the transistor tried to draw more current, the drop across R_S would cut V_GS back. (V_T = 0.7 V)

mosfet_amplifiers.caption: A common-source stage is an amplifier because its transfer curve is steep: the slope at the bias point (the gold tangent) is the gain, A_v ≈ −g_m R_D. Biasing near the steepest part of the curve gives the most gain.

mosfet_switch_node.caption: A MOSFET switch loses power two ways: conduction I²R_DS(on) while on, and switching loss each time it changes state, which grows with frequency. This sets the practical limit on converter frequency. (48 V bus, 20 ns edges.)

nodes.label: NMOS pull-down: A – B in series

cmos_logic_gates.caption: CMOS gates pair a pull-up and a pull-down network that are never on together. NAND: any 0 on an input turns on a PMOS and pulls the output high; both inputs 1 turns on the series NMOS pair and pulls it low. Only switching draws power (P = αCV²f).

amp_specs.caption: Real amplifiers lose gain at both ends: the input divides between Rs and Rin, the output between Rout and the load. High Rin and low Rout are the goal: then the overall gain approaches the no-load A_v.

miller_effect.caption: A small capacitor across an inverting amplifier looks (1 + |A_v|) times bigger at the input: C_M = Cμ(1 + |A_v|). That slows the input pole, so high gain costs bandwidth. (C_π = 10 pF.)

differential_amp.caption: A differential pair steers the tail current Iss toward whichever input is higher. Only the difference V_id matters: output ∝ tanh(V_id/2V_T), linear for |V_id| below about 20 mV.

current_mirror.caption: A current mirror copies I_ref (times the W/L ratio m) to the output. It stays near-constant once V_out passes the compliance voltage; the slope is 1/r_o with r_o ≈ V_A/I.

active_load.caption: Replacing the drain resistor with a current source makes the load resistance r_o instead of R_D, so gain jumps from g_m·R_D to about g_m·r_o/2: tens or hundreds instead of single digits.

multistage_amps.caption: Gains of cascaded stages multiply, so in decibels they simply add. But every stage adds its own bandwidth limit: three identical stages shrink the overall bandwidth to about 0.51 of one stage.

readouts.label: class B efficiency at this peak (Vcc = 10 V)

output_stages.caption: A class B push–pull stage is efficient (up to π/4 = 78.5%) but both transistors are off around zero, so the output has a dead zone: crossover distortion. A little bias (class AB, Vb→0.7 V) closes the gap at some cost in efficiency.

fns.label: V_out = A·(V₊ − V₋), limited to ±12 V

opamp_ideal.caption: An op-amp multiplies the tiny difference between its inputs by a huge gain A and then saturates at the supply. In negative feedback the output adjusts until V₊ ≈ V₋: that is the first golden rule.

inverting_amp_node.caption: Gain = −Rf/Rin: the output is an inverted, scaled copy of the input, and the inverting input stays at a virtual ground. Make Rf/Rin large enough and the output clips at the supply (±13 V).

non_inverting_amp_node.caption: Gain = 1 + Rf/Rg: the output follows the input in phase and is never smaller than the input. Rg → ∞ gives a unity-gain buffer. Large gains clip at the supply (±13 V).

summing_amp_node.caption: Each input sees its own gain Rf/Rᵢ, and the output is the inverted weighted sum. This is how audio mixers and DACs add signals. Change the gains to rebalance the mix.

integrator_node.caption: Output = −(1/RC)∫V_in dt: a constant input makes the output ramp at a steady slope, so a square wave becomes a triangle. A bigger RC gives a smaller, slower ramp.

differentiator_node.caption: Output = −RC·dV_in/dt: the output is proportional to the input’s slope, so a triangle (constant slope) becomes a square wave. Fast edges and noise are amplified, which is why real differentiators add a small series resistor.

instrumentation_amp.caption: Both inputs carry 1 V of 50 Hz hum, but the signal is only a 10 mV difference. The instrumentation amp multiplies just the difference by G = 1 + 2R/R_G and rejects the common part by its CMRR.

comparator_node.caption: A comparator has no feedback: it just reports which input is larger, swinging fully to the rail either way. Move the reference and the pulse width changes, which is the basis of PWM generators and zero-crossing detectors.

schmitt_trigger_node.caption: A Schmitt trigger has two thresholds ±V_H = ±5·R₁/(R₁+R₂). The output only flips high above +V_H and low below −V_H, so noise near a single threshold cannot make it chatter. The gap between paths is the hysteresis loop.

opamp_nonideal.caption: A real op-amp output cannot change faster than its slew rate SR. For a sine of peak Vp that limits full-power bandwidth to f = SR/(2πVp). Gain-bandwidth GBW also trades gain for speed: BW = GBW/gain.

negative_feedback_ee.caption: Negative feedback trades raw gain for precision: once Aβ ≫ 1 the closed-loop gain locks to 1/β no matter how large or drifty the open-loop gain A is.

feedback_stability_margins.caption: Phase margin tells you how far the loop is from oscillating. Rule of thumb ζ ≈ PM/100: at 20° the step response rings hard, at 60° it is well behaved, at 0° it would oscillate forever.

oscillators_ee.caption: A Wien-bridge oscillator needs loop gain 1 at f = 1/(2πRC): amplifier gain of 3. Slightly more (G > 3) lets a tiny noise signal grow until the output clips; slightly less and it dies out.

active_filters.caption: A Sallen–Key low-pass uses one op-amp (gain K) to turn a passive RC ladder into a sharp 2nd-order filter with Q = 1/(3 − K). Raising K peaks the response at the cut-off; K → 3 oscillates.

adc_basics.caption: An ADC rounds the voltage to one of 2ᴺ levels. Each extra bit halves the step (the LSB), reducing quantisation noise by 6 dB: SNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB for a full-scale sine.

dac_basics.caption: A 4-bit DAC turns each code 0–15 into one of 16 voltages (code/16)·V_ref. The steps are the converter’s resolution: more bits, finer steps. (A binary-weighted or R-2R ladder sums currents to do this.)

linear_regulators.caption: A linear regulator holds V_out by burning the excess voltage as heat: P = (V_in − V_out)·I. Its efficiency is just V_out/V_in, so a big input-to-output gap at high current gets hot quickly.

boolean_algebra_digital.caption: Absorption: A + AB = A. The B input is irrelevant (try it): the output always equals A, so the extra AND gate can be deleted. Boolean algebra shrinks circuits this way.

quine_mccluskey.caption: f = Σm(4, 8, 10, 11, 12, 15) + d(9, 14). Quine–McCluskey finds all the prime implicants (the coloured groups) and picks a minimal cover: F = AB′ + AC + BC′D′. Don’t-cares (×) may join a group if that helps.

muxes_decoders.caption: A 2-to-4 decoder with enable: output Y2 is high only when E = 1 and the address AB = 10. Each of the four outputs decodes one address; a multiplexer is the same idea in reverse.

adders_arithmetic.caption: A ripple-carry adder passes the carry through every bit, so delay grows linearly with width. Carry-lookahead computes carries in parallel groups, so delay grows only with log₄(n). (Each full-adder stage: S = A⊕B⊕C_in, C_out = AB + C_in(A⊕B).)

alu_design.caption: An ALU takes two operands and an operation select and produces a result plus status flags (zero, carry). Here is a 4-bit add/subtract unit: set A, B and op and watch the result wrap around modulo 16.

latches.caption: An SR latch remembers one bit: S sets Q to 1, R resets it to 0, and holding (repeating the same input) keeps the old value. Watch it store its state between inputs.

flip_flops.caption: A D flip-flop samples D only at the clock’s rising edge and holds it until the next edge. D can wiggle freely between edges, yet Q stays steady. That is how a clocked system remembers.

registers_counters.caption: A counter is a chain of flip-flops, each toggling at half the rate of the one before: Q0, Q1, Q2 count 0…7 in binary and each stage divides the clock by 2. Slow the clock to see each output frequency.

timing_analysis.caption: Between two flip-flops the data must travel clock-to-Q (0.4 ns) + logic + setup (0.2) + skew (0.2) before the next edge: T_clk ≥ t_cq + t_logic + t_setup + t_skew. Slow the logic or speed the clock until the line turns red.

memory_rom_ram.caption: A memory is a grid of bit cells with a decoder that turns an n-bit address into one row, and amplifiers that read the row out. Each extra address bit doubles the capacity. (SRAM cell: 6 transistors; DRAM: 1 transistor + capacitor; ROM: fixed.)

flash_memory.caption: Trapped charge on the floating gate shifts the transistor’s threshold. At the read voltage an erased cell conducts (reads 1) and a programmed cell does not (reads 0). More trapped charge means a bigger shift, which MLC/TLC flash uses to store several bits.

programmable_logic.caption: An FPGA’s basic cell is a look-up table: a small memory whose address is the input signals. Here are 8 bits for a 3-input LUT: bit k is the output when the inputs spell k in binary. Only bit 7 set = a 3-input AND; click bits to program any function.

hdl_design_flow.caption: HDL design is a loop: write RTL, simulate it, synthesise it into gates, place and route, check timing, then program the chip. A failed simulation or timing check sends you back to the code.

isa_risc_cisc.caption: The “iron law” time = instructions × cycles per instruction × clock period. CISC uses fewer, richer instructions with higher CPI; RISC uses more, simpler ones with CPI near 1. Neither wins by definition: it depends on the numbers.

assembly_language.caption: Assembly is one human-readable line per machine instruction: a C statement becomes load, add and store instructions, and the assembler turns each line into a binary word (here a 16-bit Thumb ADDS: opcode 0001100, Rm = 2, Rn = 1, Rd = 0).

datapath_control.caption: The datapath moves and transforms data (PC, instruction fetch, registers, ALU, memory, write-back); the control unit reads the opcode and tells each part what to do this cycle. Follow a token through one instruction.

pipelining_hazards.caption: Pipelining overlaps instructions like an assembly line: after the 4-cycle fill, one instruction finishes per cycle. A data hazard (i3 needs a load result) forces a one-cycle bubble; the later instructions all slip one column.

cache_memory.caption: AMAT = t_hit + miss rate × t_miss. Because a miss costs ~100× a hit, even a few percent of misses dominate the average. Better hit rates matter more than a slightly faster cache.

memory_hierarchy.caption: Each level is bigger, slower and cheaper than the one above it. From a register to a hard disk the access time spans about 7 orders of magnitude: caches exist because programs reuse nearby data.

virtual_memory.caption: Every address a program uses is virtual. The top bits (page number) are translated through a page table (here: frame = (5·page + 3) mod 16) to a physical frame; the low bits (offset within the 4 KiB page) pass straight through. Slide the address across a page boundary.

mcu_architecture.caption: A microcontroller is a whole computer on one chip: a CPU core, flash for the program, SRAM for data, and peripherals (GPIO, serial ports, converters, timers) all sharing a bus. ARM Cortex-M, AVR and PIC differ in detail, not in this layout.

gpio.caption: A GPIO pin is a switchable output (and readable input). To light an LED you need a series resistor to set the current, I = (V_DD − V_F)/R; most pins can only supply about 20 mA. (LED forward drop assumed 2 V.)

interrupts.caption: An interrupt lets hardware demand attention instead of the program polling. The CPU saves where it was, runs a short service routine (ISR), then resumes. The cost is CPU time: load = rate × ISR time.

timers_pwm.caption: A timer counts clock ticks and flips the pin when it matches a compare value; the fraction of the period spent high is the duty cycle D. A filter or a motor sees the average V_avg = D·V_cc: a fake analog voltage from a digital pin.

mcu_adc_dac.caption: An MCU’s ADC turns a voltage into an integer: code = floor(V_in/V_ref × 2ᴺ) with V_ref = 3.3 V, and its DAC does the reverse. More bits give finer steps, but the extra codes only help if noise stays below one LSB.

uart_serial.caption: UART has no clock wire. The line idles high; a falling start bit begins a frame, then 8 data bits (least-significant first) and a stop bit, each lasting 1/baud. Change the byte and watch the pattern change.

readouts.label: bits per second at 8 MHz clock

spi_bus.caption: SPI sends a byte with a shared clock: pull CS low, then the master puts one bit on MOSI before each rising SCLK edge (most-significant bit first) and the slave samples it. Four wires, no addresses, very fast.

i2c_bus.caption: I²C lines are open-drain: devices only pull them low, and a pull-up resistor lets them rise. The rise time is set by R·C of the wire, so more devices or longer wires (bigger C) cap the speed; a smaller pull-up helps but wastes current.

can_bus.caption: CAN sends each bit as the difference between two wires: dominant (0) is about 2 V apart, recessive (1) is 0 V. Noise hits both wires equally, so it cancels in the difference. The lowest arbitration ID wins the bus.

usb_protocol.caption: USB power grew from 2.5 W (5 V at 0.5 A) to 240 W with PD 3.1 (48 V at 5 A). Higher power works by raising the voltage: the same cable current carries more watts.

rtos.caption: Rate-monotonic scheduling guarantees all deadlines if total CPU utilisation U ≤ n(2^(1/n) − 1), which falls from 1 toward ln 2 ≈ 0.69 as tasks are added. Below the curve you are safe; above it you must check more carefully.

fns.label: dynamic power P = C V² f [mW]

low_power_design.caption: Dynamic power P = C·V²·f grows with the square of the supply voltage, so dropping V is the most powerful trick: half the voltage means a quarter of the power. Lower the clock for a further linear saving.

device_drivers.caption: A driver hides a device’s messy details behind a clean interface: the application just calls read() or write(); the driver pokes the device registers and handles the interrupt when the hardware is ready.

interfacing_sensors.caption: A thermistor’s resistance falls as it warms (R = R₀ e^(B(1/T − 1/T₀)), 10 kΩ at 25 °C). In a divider with a 10 kΩ resistor that becomes a voltage the ADC can read. The steeper the curve, the better the sensitivity.

interfacing_motors.caption: A PWM duty cycle scales a DC motor’s supply voltage. Speed falls linearly with load torque, and the stall torque and no-load speed both scale with D. Peak mechanical power is a quarter of (no-load speed × stall torque).

interfacing_displays.caption: A 7-segment digit is seven LEDs a–g. Choosing which segments to light shows a number; to drive many digits with few pins the MCU multiplexes them, lighting one digit at a time faster than the eye can see. A 4-digit display at 1 kHz refresh updates each digit 250 times a second.
